overview:
Reuben and Gad, rich in cattle, see that the conquered land of Jazer and Gilead is good pasture and ask Moses to let them settle there without crossing the Jordan. Moses hears Kadesh-barnea all over again, when the spies' report turned the people back and a generation died in the wilderness. The two tribes answer with an offer: they will build folds for the flocks and towns for their families, then march armed ahead of Israel and stay until every tribe has its land. Moses accepts on that condition, binds Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads to enforce it, and grants them the kingdoms of Sihon and Og. Clans of Manasseh take northern Gilead.

The proverb “be sure your sin will find you out” (v. 23) comes from this chapter. Moses says it to two tribes who have not yet sinned, as a warning about a promise they might fail to keep.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars see Numbers as compiled later from older and priestly sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The fortieth year after the Exodus, after the war with Midian (31:1–12). Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 puts it about 1406 BC; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The camp on the plains of Moab; the land in question is the tableland north of the Arnon and the hills of Gilead, taken from Sihon and Og (21:21–35).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Deuteronomy 3:12–20 (Moses recalls the grant and the condition); Joshua 13:8–32 (the eastern tribes' borders).

hermeneutics:
The Mesha Stele, set up about 840 BC and found at Dibon in 1868, names many of this chapter's towns from the Moabite side: Ataroth, Dibon, Nebo, Baal-meon, Kiriathaim, Aroer, Jahaz. Mesha says the men of Gad had lived in “the country of Ataroth from ancient times,” and that the king of Israel fortified it before Mesha took it back. Gad's hold on the tableland was remembered even by its enemies, and the land Moses grants here was still contested centuries later. Dibon, which Gad builds in v. 34, became Mesha's own capital.

The tableland between the Arnon and Heshbon is open, rolling country with enough rain for grain and grass, and it was sheep country in antiquity. Second Kings 3:4 calls Mesha a “sheepmaster” who paid Israel a hundred thousand lambs a year. Reuben and Gad choose the land as herders choose (vv. 1, 4), and their first plan is stone folds for the flocks (v. 16). Excavation has complicated the picture at some sites: Tell Hesban (Heshbon) and Dhiban (Dibon) have yielded little or nothing from the Late Bronze Age, one reason scholars debate when the conquest stories took shape.

Renaming a captured town marked a change of owner. Shalmaneser III of Assyria took Til-Barsip on the Euphrates in 856 BC and renamed it Kar-Shalmaneser, “Fort Shalmaneser.” The chapter ends with the same move three times over: the Reubenites give their cities “other names” (v. 38), Jair calls his villages Havoth-jair, “the tent-villages of Jair” (v. 41), and Nobah renames Kenath after himself (v. 42).

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence. It is a negotiation, and the terms are restated until both sides have said them in public.

rows.text: Moses repeats them to the leaders

notes: **“Before the LORD”:** the Hebrew phrase comes 7 times in vv. 20–32 (vv. 20, 21, 22 twice, 27, 29, 32). The tribes first offer to march “before the children of Israel” (v. 17); in the terms the army marches before the LORD. KJV has an eighth in v. 22, where the Hebrew says “from the LORD.”

**Kadesh retold:** Moses' speech (vv. 8–13) compresses chs. 13–14. The verb “discourage” frames it (vv. 7, 9), and those who “have not wholly followed” are set against Caleb and Joshua, who have (vv. 11–12).

The request follows the defeat of Midian and the earlier conquest of Sihon and Og (21:21–35). The land is already taken; the question is who will live in it. This is the first tribal settlement in the book, and it lies outside the borders of Canaan as ch. 34 draws them (34:13–15).

**Forward:** Joshua sends the eastern tribes home with praise for keeping this promise (Joshua 22:1–4), and their altar by the Jordan nearly starts a war over whether they still belong to Israel (Joshua 22:10–34).

traditions.text: Philo notes that the two tribes were a sixth of the whole army and that they were already living in the well-watered land they asked for. He gives Moses a long speech asking whether they will sit at ease while their kinsmen fight: “ye are one race, ye have the same fathers.” The tribes answer that they fear no hard service and ask only to leave families and herds behind walls, and Philo says they then marched out more eagerly than anyone, as men repaying a gift already received.

Josephus includes the half tribe of Manasseh in the original request. He has Moses call them cowards who had invented the cattle as a decent excuse for avoiding the war while others labored for the land. The tribes reply that they want their prey and families in safe places so that they can fight unencumbered. Moses then grants the land of the Amorites before Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal chiefs on that condition, and they build strong cities for their wives, children, and goods.

Moses states the deal both ways: if the tribes cross, they get Gilead; if not, they take land in Canaan (vv. 29–30). Rabbi Meir made this the model for conditional agreements such as betrothals: a condition that does not spell out both outcomes, as Moses did with Gad and Reuben, is no condition at all. Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel disagreed, arguing that the negative half was needed here only so that no one would think the tribes would lose their share in Canaan too.

The phrase “guiltless before the LORD, and before Israel” (v. 22) became a rule for Temple officials. The man who drew coins from the treasury chamber could not wear a hemmed garment, shoes, sandals, phylacteries, or an amulet, anything that might hide a coin. If he later grew poor, people might call it punishment for theft, and if he grew rich, they might say he had stolen. A person must appear innocent to people as well as to God, and the Mishnah cites this verse as its proof.

The midrash notices that the tribes offer folds for cattle before cities for children (v. 16), and that Moses hands the plan back the other way round (v. 24): put first things first. It sets wealth beside wisdom and strength as gifts that last only when they come from God. Because Reuben and Gad loved their possessions and separated from their brothers to keep them, it says, they were the first tribes taken into exile, citing 1 Chronicles 5:26.
traditions.cite: Numbers Rabbah 22:7, 9; Tanhuma Mattot 7; Rashi on 32:16

traditions.text: Rashi reads “do that which hath proceeded out of your mouth” (v. 24) as treating the tribes' words as a vow, like the vows of ch. 30, and as holding them to more than Moses asked. Moses required them to stay only until the land was subdued (v. 22), but they had promised to stay until every Israelite had his inheritance (v. 18). Rashi counts that as seven more years west of the Jordan while the land was divided.

Explaining “their names being changed” (v. 38), Rashi says Nebo and Baal-meon were names of idols, since the people of the land named their cities after their gods, so the Reubenites gave them new names. He identifies Shibmah in v. 38 with Shebam in v. 3. On Nobah's naming of Kenath (v. 42), he reports an earlier teacher's view that an unusual spelling hints the name did not last, and then questions that argument himself.

This Aramaic paraphrase replaces the town names with ones its readers knew and fills them with history. In v. 3 and v. 38 it renders Nebo as the place of Moses' grave, looking ahead to Deuteronomy 34. It turns Baal-meon into the city of Balak, rebuilt after the idol of Peor was torn out of it, and says the builders then named the towns after themselves.

Eusebius locates several of the chapter's towns in the Roman province of Arabia. Heshbon is “now called Esbus,” a well-known city; Elealeh belongs to Reuben; Baal-meon is the town “which the sons of Ruben built”; Jazer marks the border of Ammon near Philadelphia (modern Amman); Mount Nebo is pointed out about six miles west of Heshbon. His entries show the names of Numbers 32 still in use some fifteen centuries later.
